rv.q: The painting forms the matrix of Rockets and Blue Lights, Pinnock’s inspirationally ambitious and all-encompassingly humane examination of the unresolved history of the transatlantic slave trade.
Miranda Cromwell’s production – which was shut down after its third performance at Manchester’s Royal Exchange in March 2020 – feels urgent and important.
The wealth of overlapping stories – several about storytelling itself – give the drama an exciting, anarchic edge but also create cerebral circles within circles...
But, personally speaking, I could never quite grasp the full shape of what Pinnock and Crowell were creating.
The play is a sprawling piece of work, and the pacing is oddly modulated, with a first half that takes its time setting up its chess pieces, and a second that lands only some of its gut-punches.
In effect, there are three or four playlets competing for our attention, and none of them comes to life.
In a theatrical climate defined over the last year by solo or small-cast plays, here is writing that thinks big.

Most of all, in a theatrical landscape that loves to produce American stories about the Black experience, it is a thrill to see a play that directly and explicitly confronts Britain's history with the slave trade, and the legacy of enslavement for English descendants of colonial brutality.
This tsunami of piffle will serve at least one sociopolitical function.
Pinnock and director Miranda Cromwell have certainly packed this production full of political interrogation.

cn.t: Pinnock's ambitious play about slavery's legacy and Turner's painting offers powerful ideas and strong performances, but critics find it overstuffed with plotlines and characters, resulting in mixed reception despite its timely themes.
